playbook:
When a new common-resource game starts, I compute the total sustainable extraction (stock × regrowth rate, split across players) and treat that as my default only as a hypothesis to be tested in season 1, not a commitment. The old plan — a modest early grab capped so the stock survives even if everyone grabs hard — fails because "modest" still leaves me behind when everyone's actual grab is larger. Both defecting episodes I have now seen had at least one boat taking well above share from the very first season; nobody starts cooperative and drifts.

I now treat the opening grab as a signal-gathering move sized near the top of the cooperative range, not above it: big enough that I am not the chump if everyone's racing, small enough that the stock clearly survives if everyone matches. After season 1's numbers land, I commit fully to whichever regime the data show — no middle course.

With three or more boats, expect the worst-case from round one. In this episode all three boats grabbed hard simultaneously (54 landed from a 100 stock in season 1), and the fishery was effectively terminal after two seasons despite 50% regrowth. Group defection kills the stock faster than a single defector does, so my two-season patience window only applies when restraint is actually mutual or near-mutual. If season 1 total extraction already exceeded the sustainable total, I skip the patience phase entirely and move straight to the race.

Unilateral conservation against any persistent defector does not work, and this episode confirms it from the other side: everyone raced, the stock collapsed to 15.8 by season 3, and the last three seasons yielded almost nothing for anyone. The total landed across the fleet was far below what a cooperative path would have produced — but since I can't enforce cooperation, my choice is only between racing early and racing late. Race early.

My season-1 read decides everything: if total landed ≤ roughly the sustainable total, I continue at share and extend trust another season; if total landed clearly exceeds it, I immediately switch to proportional-share racing and never look back. There is no third option where my restraint persuades anyone — I have never seen it work.

When I model the danger zone, I track the worst player's extraction rate, not the average. If one player consistently takes an amount that, combined with even moderate takes from others, exhausts the stock in N seasons, I plan for collapse at season N and make sure I've banked my share before then. With regrowth of r, the sustainable total is r×stock/(1+r) — compute it exactly rather than guessing.

Matching the sustainable share is only my strategy when others match it too. The moment the data show the group defecting, the value of looking cooperative drops to near zero — the fishery ends in a race whether I join it or not, so I'd rather join it in season 2 than season 4.

In a confirmed race, each season I take roughly my proportional share (stock ÷ number of boats active), adjusted: a bit more if others are out-grabbing their share, a bit less only if taking my full share would itself zero the stock. A fixed cautious number like 7 from a 15.8 stock just donates the difference to whoever grabs 5; proportional keeps pace.

In the endgame (final season, or any season where the stock will be dead before meaningful regrowth), I take as much as can be safely landed: roughly stock minus what I expect others to grab, computed so my submission cannot be zeroed out. I want to arrive at that moment having already banked a healthy total, which is what early racing achieves.

Every submission, I run the arithmetic: current stock, expected extraction by each other boat (using their observed pattern, not the cooperative ideal), regrowth of the remainder, and seasons left. I only under-take the sustainable share when the model — built from observed behavior — shows the group as a whole is on a survivable path.

One honesty check on my racing grabs: in this episode my season-2 take of 17 from a 55.5 stock was about right proportionally, but my season-1 take of 18 while others took 20–25 meant I started the race already behind. When the opening confirms a race, the proportional share from a full stock is stock/boats (≈33 here, capped by what all-three-grabbing would leave alive) — next time I calibrate the opening grab to that ceiling, not to a "modest" figure above sustainable.

1.text:
On the opening season I harvest above the sustainable share because early fish are worth more than future fish, but I now treat my opener as a signal as well as a take: a very large first catch invites rivals to escalate in season 2 and beyond. I'll open strong but not at the top of the plausible range — enough to bank early fish without teaching everyone the fishery is already a strip-mining contest. In practice, aiming slightly above the top of sustainable rather than at ~25% of the stock is the better bid.

I still leave enough on the table that even greedy rivals cannot zero the stock in one season, and I extend that check: before every submission I simulate the worst case where both rivals match or slightly exceed my take, and I size my catch so the fishery survives that round.

When I see revealed catches above sustainable, I no longer match escalation blindly. I first ask who is causing the decline. If rivals' takes are stable or falling while the stock still crashes, my own share is part of the problem and matching just accelerates the collapse everyone loses to. I match only when rivals are escalating *and* the stock has enough buffer that the race is worth running.

Once a rival backs off noticeably, that is my opening: I increase my share of the remaining take rather than also retreating, because their restraint is a donation I should collect, sized so the regrowth isn't fully cancelled while seasons remain to profit from it.

I watch the season-2 responses as the critical read on the table. If rivals respond to my opener with high takes, I assume the fishery will be depleted by mid-game and I shift immediately from "manage the stock" to "bank fish faster than they do." A cooperative recovery is a bonus, not a plan.

When the stock falls to a small fraction of capacity with several seasons left, I stop thinking about the sustainable share entirely — it is tiny and regrowth from a low base won't rebuild in time. I compute what the fishery yields if everyone grabs, and I take a large share of what remains now, checking only that my grab plus plausible rival grabs leaves something above zero so the final season still exists.

With two or fewer seasons left, fractional fish are nearly worthless: I take a large share of what remains, enough that even if rivals grab hard there is still enough left for a meaningful final sweep.

On the final season, I abandon all conservation and submit for the entire remaining stock — leftovers score nobody anything. I keep this habit regardless of how the game has gone.

I never trust that a depleted stock will recover before the game ends; when remaining seasons are few relative to regrowth time, current fish beat future fish and I front-load.

I verify each season that my submitted catch is what I intended before sending, I track the running total, and I sanity-check the arithmetic: stock minus all submitted catches, then regrowth at 50% capped at capacity, so I know exactly how much runway my take leaves.

2.text:
When the pool is large and regrowth is strong, I take above the sustainable share early — roughly 1.5–2× the stated share — because early fish are worth the most while the stock is high, but never so much that my own catch alone risks zeroing the fishery. Early aggression paid off again: nearly all of my total came from the first three seasons, because the fishery was effectively dead by season 4.

New this game: the collapse can come much faster than expected. With two heavy grabbers (boat 1 at 17–25, boat 3 at 18–25), the stock went from 100 to 15.8 in two seasons. So I treat season 1's revealed landings as the key diagnostic: if the other boats' combined take is clearly above sustainable, I assume the fishery has only two or three good seasons left and I front-load accordingly. My season-2 take of 10 while they took 17–18 was too timid — against multiple defectors I should match or exceed the largest defector's take while stock remains, not settle for 1.5× a share that no one else is respecting.

When I see the season's total landings and the new stock figure, I identify each boat's behavior pattern, not just the average. Persistent defectors are treated as fixed grabbers in my forecasts; I never assume they will cooperate later.

Restraint against defectors is a losing move, and this episode confirmed it again: restraint only has value if it can actually stabilize the stock. Before switching to restraint, I compute whether stock minus (my sustainable take + the defectors' expected takes) still leaves the fishery collapsing. If it does, I take at least the defectors' level to claim fish before they destroy them, rather than dying virtuous. With two defectors the answer is almost always "collapsing."

Against a cooperative or mixed field I still consider near-sustainable harvesting, but only when the arithmetic shows my restraint plus plausible others keeps the fishery viable past the mid-game.

When the final season comes — or when the stock is so low the fishery is effectively over — I take roughly my one-third split of the entire remaining stock, since fish left in the water at the end are worth zero. This time the fishery died before the official final season; next time I recognize "effective final season" earlier by checking whether expected total landings will zero or near-zero the stock, and grab my share that season rather than waiting for season 6.

I never submit zero or a token amount while the fishery is alive, and I never take so much alone that my own catch could zero the stock before the endgame unless my share of the remainder would exceed it anyway.

I keep the arithmetic straight each season: post-catch stock = current stock minus total landings; next stock = 1.5 × that, capped at the maximum. I use this both to test whether a planned over-harvest is survivable and to forecast the collapse date under others' observed behavior, so I know how many harvesting seasons I actually have left.
